claim: Hyperexcitability has been suggested to contribute to motoneuron degeneration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Hyperexcitability has been suggested to contribute to motoneuron degeneration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
evidence: This is a statement about what has been suggested in the literature, supported by the review citation.

claim: The most vulnerable motoneurons in ALS become unable to fire repetitively despite functional neuromuscular junctions.
source: We found that, far from being hyperexcitable, the most vulnerable motoneurons become unable to fire repetitively despite the fact that their neuromuscular junctions were still functional.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by electrophysiological recordings and motor unit testing.

claim: Intrinsic hyperexcitability is unlikely to be the cause of motoneuron degeneration in ALS.
source: Our results indicate that intrinsic hyperexcitability is unlikely to be the cause of motoneuron degeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing hypoexcitability rather than hyperexcitability in vulnerable motoneurons.

claim: Changes in excitability occur very early in mutant superoxide dismutase 1 (mSOD1) mice.
source: In fact, changes in excitability occur very early in mutant superoxide dismutase 1 (mSOD1) mice, a standard model of ALS.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mSOD1 embryos, spinal motoneurons are hyperexcitable.
source: In mSOD1 embryos, spinal motoneurons are hyperexcitable (Pieri et al., 2003; Kuo et al., 2005; Martin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three previous studies.

claim: In neonates, motoneuron excitability was found to be increased (hyperexcitable) in some studies.
source: In neonates, motoneuron excitability was found to be increased (hyperexcitable) in some studies (van Zundert et al., 2008; Elbasiouny et al., 2010; Leroy et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies showing hyperexcitability in neonates.

claim: In neonates, motoneuron excitability was found to be unaltered in some studies.
source: In neonates, motoneuron excitability was found to be increased (hyperexcitable) in some studies (van Zundert et al., 2008; Elbasiouny et al., 2010; Leroy et al., 2014), unaltered in others (Pambo-Pambo et al., 2009; Quinlan et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies showing no change in excitability.

claim: A decrease in input resistance was reported in neonatal motoneurons, suggesting hypoexcitability.
source: and in Bories et al. (2007), a decrease in input resistance was reported, suggesting that spinal motoneurons became hypoexcitable.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study showing decreased input resistance.

claim: In adults before the onset of degeneration, a substantial fraction of motoneurons lose their ability to elicit a repetitive discharge in response to sustained inputs.
source: At a later time point, in adults, before the onset of degeneration, we reported that a substantial fraction of motoneurons lose their ability to elicit a repetitive discharge in response to sustained inputs (Delestrée et al., 2014), a clear manifestation of hypoexcitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The remaining motoneurons that still produced a repetitive discharge retained normal excitability.
source: The remaining motoneurons, which still produced a repetitive discharge, retained normal excitability (Delestrée et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Studies in motoneurons derived from human iPSCs confirmed a tendency for excitability to shift from hyperexcitable to hypoexcitable during the course of the disease.
source: Studies in motoneurons derived from human iPSCs confirmed this tendency for excitability to shift from a hyperexcitable (Wainger et al., 2014) to a hypoexcitable state (Sareen et al., 2014; Devlin et al., 2015; Naujock et al., 2016) during the course of the disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four studies on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claim: The most vulnerable motoneurons in ALS are those of the largest motor units that innervate fast-contracting and fatigable muscle fibers (FF type).
source: The most vulnerable and the first to degenerate are the motoneurons of the largest motor units that innervate the fast-contracting and fatigable muscle fibers (FF type), followed by the motoneurons of intermediate motor unit size, which innervate the fast-contracting and fatigue-resistant muscle fibers (FR type).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on motor unit vulnerability.

claim: Motoneurons of intermediate motor unit size that innervate fast-contracting and fatigue-resistant muscle fibers (FR type) degenerate after FF motoneurons.
source: The most vulnerable and the first to degenerate are the motoneurons of the largest motor units that innervate the fast-contracting and fatigable muscle fibers (FF type), followed by the motoneurons of intermediate motor unit size, which innervate the fast-contracting and fatigue-resistant muscle fibers (FR type).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on motor unit vulnerability patterns.

claim: Motoneurons of the smallest motor units that mainly innervate slow contracting and fatigue-resistant fibers (S type) are the most resistant and least affected at end-stage disease.
source: Finally, the motoneurons of the smallest motor units, that mainly innervate the slow contracting and fatigue-resistant fibers (S type) are the most resistant and the least affected at the end-stage of disease (Pun et al., 2006; Hegedus et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on motor unit vulnerability.

claim: Only a subgroup of motoneurons are hyperexcitable (rheobase is lowered) at P6–P10 in mSOD1 mice.
source: In a recent study, we demonstrated that only a subgroup of motoneurons are hyperexcitable (rheobase is lowered) at P6–P10 in mSOD1 mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The hyperexcitable motoneurons at P6-P10 in mSOD1 mice were identified as S-type, the most resistant in ALS.
source: However, using a combination of electrophysiological, morphological and molecular criteria, these motoneurons were identified as S-type, that is the most resistant in ALS (Leroy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The intrinsic excitability of the most vulnerable motoneurons is unchanged at P6-P10 in mSOD1 mice.
source: In sharp contrast, the intrinsic excitability of the most vulnerable motoneurons is unchanged at this age, arguing against the idea that early hyperexcitability contributes to selective degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: FF motor units lose their neuromuscular junctions around 60 days post-natal in the SOD1G93A model.
source: Nevertheless, degeneration of the most vulnerable motoneurons starts several weeks later (the FF motor units lose their neuromuscular junctions around 60 days post-natal in the SOD1G93A model; Pun et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on denervation timing.

claim: Motoneurons that failed to discharge repetitively are distributed predominantly among the FF and the largest FR motor units.
source: Our experiments revealed that motoneurons that failed to discharge repetitively in response to sustained inputs are distributed predominantly among the FF and the largest FR motor units.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Large motor units tend to become hypoexcitable over disease progression in a mouse model of FUS-ALS.
source: To do this, we repeated our experiments in a mouse model of FUS-ALS (Sharma et al., 2016) and found again that large motor units tend to become hypoexcitable over disease progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments in the FUS-ALS model.

claim: Chodl has been proposed as a marker for Fast-type motoneurons.
source: Combining in vivo electrophysiology and in situ hybridization, we have investigated the expression pattern of C-type lectin chondrolectin (Chodl) in WT mice since it has been proposed as a marker for Fast-type motoneurons (Enjin et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Chodl disappears over the course of ALS progression.
source: Combining in vivo electrophysiology and in situ hybridization, we have investigated the expression pattern of C-type lectin chondrolectin (Chodl) in WT mice since it has been proposed as a marker for Fast-type motoneurons (Enjin et al., 2010) that disappears over the course of ALS progression (Wootz et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In WT mice, Chodl is expressed in FF motoneurons and in the largest FR motoneurons, but not in small FRs.
source: In WT mice, we found that Chodl is expressed in the FF motoneurons, as well as in the largest FR motoneurons, but not in the small FRs, matching the hypoexcitability pattern in SOD1G93A mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments combining electrophysiology and in situ hybridization.

claim: FR motoneurons constitute a heterogeneous population that differentially lose their ability to fire repetitively over the course of disease progression.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that FR motoneurons constitute a heterogeneous population that differentially lose their ability to fire repetitively over the course of disease progression, a property that may underlie their differential vulnerability in ALS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on FR motoneuron properties.

claim: The expression patterns of p-eIF2α and p62 aggregates suggest that hypoexcitable motoneurons are more advanced in disease progression than those that still fire repetitively.
source: Moreover, the expression patterns of p-eIF2α and p62 aggregates suggest that the hypoexcitable motoneurons are more advanced in the disease progression than those that still fire repetitively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from immunostaining data on disease markers.

claim: In ALS mice, both FF and the largest FR motoneurons lose the fundamental property of firing repetitively prior to their degeneration.
source: We conclude that in ALS mice, both the FF and the largest FR motoneurons are not hyperexcitable prior to their degeneration, but on the contrary, lose the fundamental property of firing repetitively.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Recordings were performed on 46 to 60 days old animals (WT: 54 ± 5 days; N = 45; SOD1G93A: 52 ± 5 days; N = 36).
source: Recordings were performed on 46 to 60 days old animals (WT: 54 ± 5 days; N = 45; SOD1G93A: 52 ± 5 days; N = 36).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental subjects.

claim: The contractile properties (twitch amplitude, twitch contraction time and fatigue index) vary widely across the motor unit population but display inter-relationships in both WT and SOD1G93A animals.
source: Figure 2 shows that, despite the fact that the contractile properties (namely twitch amplitude, twitch contraction time and fatigue index) vary widely across the motor unit population, they clearly display some inter-relationships in both WT and SOD1G93A animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A cutoff value of 20 ms was used to separate 'slow' motor units from 'fast' contracting ones.
source: We chose a cutoff value of 20 ms to separate those 'slow' motor units from the 'fast' contracting ones.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the data distribution.

claim: All motor units with a contraction time longer than 20 ms developed a weak twitch force (all but one under 1.0 mN).
source: Indeed, all the motor units with a contraction time longer than 20 ms developed a weak twitch force (all but one under 1.0 mN: WT: 0.7 ± 0.5 mN; [0.2–1.8 mN]; N = 8; SOD1G93A: 0.4 ± 0.3 mN; [0.1–1.1 mN]; N = 12; Figure 2A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 2A1.

claim: Fast motor units (contraction time shorter than 20 ms) displayed a much wider range of twitch force.
source: In contrast, the fast motor units (contraction time shorter than 20 ms) displayed a much wider range of twitch force (WT: 3.8 ± 5.4 mN; [0.1–29.8 mN]; N = 98; SOD1G93A: 5.9 ± 10.3 mN; [0.1–53.1 mN]; N = 80; Figure 2A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 2A1.

claim: Motor units with a contraction time longer than 20 ms were all fatigue resistant (fatigue index between 0.86 and 1.00 in both WT and SOD1G93A mice).
source: Motor units with a contraction time longer than 20 ms were all fatigue resistant (fatigue index between 0.86 and 1.00 in both WT and SOD1G93A mice, Figure 2A2 and B2; see also the slow-contracting motor unit in Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A2, 2B2, and 1C.

claim: All of the fatigable motor units (fatigue index below 0.5) developed a large initial amount of twitch force.
source: However, all of the fatigable motor units (fatigue index below 0.5) developed a large initial amount of twitch force (e.g. 12.7 mN for the motor unit in Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data and an example from Figure 1A.

claim: Fast-contracting, fatigue resistant (FR) units can be distinguished from fast-contracting, fatigable (FF) units using a cut-off value of 8 mN.
source: Remarkably, with very few exceptions, we were able to distinguish fast contracting, fatigue resistant (FR) from fast-contracting, fatigable (FF) units a cut-off value of 8 mN (Figure 2A3 and B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A3 and 2B3.

claim: In WT mice, 13 motor units were classified as FF (12%), 85 as FR (80%) and eight as S (8%).
source: In WT mice, we classified 13 motor units as FF (12%), 85 as FR (80%) and eight as S (8%).
evidence: This is a summary of the classification results from the study.

claim: In SOD1G93A mice, 15 units were classified as FF (16%), 65 as FR (71%) and 12 as S (13%).
source: In SOD1G93A mice, we classified 15 units as FF (16%), 65 as FR (71%) and 12 as S (13%).
evidence: This is a summary of the classification results from the study.

claim: The proportions of motor units of each type found in WT vs. SOD1G93A mice were not statistically different.
source: The proportions of motor units of each type found in WT vs. SOD1G93A mice were not statistically different (χ2 test p=0.28)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: FF motor units display a slightly longer contraction time in mutant mice.
source: We observed that FF motor units display a slightly longer contraction time in mutant mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The longer contraction time in FF motor units might reflect a desynchronization of their muscle fibers that precedes denervation proper.
source: Since these units develop a similar amount of force as in control mice (Table 1), this might reflect a desynchronization of their muscle fibers that precedes denervation proper.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claim: A substantial fraction of SOD1G93A motoneurons was not able to discharge in response to a ramp, despite being able to fire at the onset of a square pulse.
source: As we previously described (Delestrée et al., 2014), a substantial fraction of motoneurons was not able to discharge in response to the ramp, despite the fact that they were still able to fire at the onset of a square pulse (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to previous work.

claim: The loss of repetitive firing is a manifestation of hypoexcitability of motoneurons.
source: This lack of repetitive firing is a manifestation of hypoexcitability of these motoneurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established understanding of neuronal excitability.

claim: The loss of function occurs before the denervation of the neuromuscular junctions.
source: Notably, this loss of function occurs before the denervation of the neuromuscular junctions as every cell in this study was able to activate its muscle fibers (as shown by the recording of a motor unit action potential at the surface of the muscle) and to produce a twitch in response to a spike elicited by a short pulse of current (Figure 3A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing functional neuromuscular junctions.

claim: The loss of function was significantly more frequent in SOD1G93A motoneurons than in WT motoneurons (21% vs. 6%).
source: The loss of function was significantly more frequent in SOD1G93A motoneurons than in WT motoneurons (21% vs. 6%, exact Fisher test p=0.01, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Non-firing motoneurons were more prevalent in the largest motor units.
source: Moreover, non-firing motoneurons were not distributed homogeneously in all physiological types of motor units, but were more prevalent in the largest units (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: In SOD1G93A mice, 40% of the FF units (6/15 tested) were unable to fire repetitively.
source: In SOD1G93A mice, 40% of the FF units (6/15 tested) were unable to fire repetitively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: Among FR units in SOD1G93A mice, 20% (11/55 tested) were unable to fire repetitively, but all non-firing cells were among the largest FR motor units (1.5–4.0 mN).
source: Among the FR units, 20% (11/55 tested) were unable to fire repetitively, but all the non-firing cells were among the largest FR motor unit (1.5–4.0 mN)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: 46% of the large FR units (11/24 tested) in SOD1G93A mice were unable to fire repetitively.
source: if we split the FR population in two along the median (1.3 mN), 46% of the large FR (11/24 tested) were unable to fire repetitively
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: 100% of the small FR units in SOD1G93A mice fired repetitively (31/31 tested).
source: whereas 100% of the small FR units fired repetitively (31/31 tested).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: All S units in SOD1G93A mice were able to fire repetitively (8/8 tested).
source: Similarly, all the S units were able to fire repetitively (8/8 tested).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: The motor units that did not fire repetitively developed significantly more force than those that were able to fire repetitively, regardless of genotype.
source: ANOVA analysis confirmed that the motor units that did not fire repetitively developed significantly more force than those that were able to fire repetitively, regardless of the genotype (p<0.001, Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The motoneurons' input conductances were, on average, larger in FF motor units than in FRs, which were in turn larger than in slow motoneurons.
source: As expected, the motoneurons' input conductances were, on average, larger in FF motor units than in FRs, which were in turn larger than in slow motoneurons (one-way ANOVA, p<0.0001; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The motoneurons that were unable to discharge repetitively had a larger input conductance than those that still fired repetitively, regardless of genotype.
source: The motoneurons that were unable to discharge repetitively had a larger input conductance than those that still fired repetitively, regardless of the genotype (two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001; Figure 3G)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The motoneurons that did not fire repetitively had an average resting membrane potential more depolarized than those that did, regardless of genotype.
source: Interestingly, the motoneurons that did not fire repetitively had an average resting membrane potential more depolarized than those that did, regardless of their genotype (two-way ANOVA, p=0.01)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Non-repetitively-firing SOD1G93A motoneurons had an average resting membrane potential of −62 ± 8 mV (N = 17).
source: non-repetitively-firing SOD1G93A motoneurons had an average resting membrane potential of −62 ± 8 mV (N = 17)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: SOD1G93A motoneurons that fired repetitively rested at −68 ± 8 mV (N = 63).
source: while those that fired repetitively rested at −68 ± 8 mV (N = 63)(Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The largest motor units (FF and FR larger than 1.3 mN) were more depolarized in SOD1G93A mice than in controls.
source: Overall, we observed that the largest motor units (FF and FR larger than 1.3 mN) were more depolarized in SOD1G93A mice than in controls (Table 2)
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: The recruitment current is linearly related to the input conductance of the motoneuron.
source: The recruitment current is linearly related to the input conductance of the motoneuron: the larger the input conductance, the larger the recruitment current (Figure 4A, r2 = 0.81, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The recruitment current was on average larger in FF motoneurons than in FRs, which was in turn larger than in S motoneurons.
source: Therefore, similarly to the input conductance, the recruitment current was on average larger in the FF motoneurons than in the FRs, where it was, in turn, larger than in the S motoneurons (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, p<0.0001; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The recruitment current was unchanged for all motoneuron types in SOD1G93A mice compared with WT mice.
source: Compared with WT mice, the recruitment current was unchanged for all motoneuron types in SOD1G93A mice compared with the WT mice (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: The slope of the relationship between recruitment current and input conductance was not significantly different between WT and SOD1G93A motoneurons.
source: Comparing WT and SOD1G93A motoneurons, we found that the slope of the relationship between the recruitment current and the input conductance was not significantly different (ANCOVA p=0.99, Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The excitability of motoneurons that retain the ability to fire repetitively was unaffected by the mutation.
source: indicating that the excitability of the motoneurons that retain the ability to fire repetitively was unaffected by the mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of recruitment current data.

claim: The voltage excursion was unaffected in SOD1G93A vs. WT motoneurons.
source: The voltage excursion (difference between the spiking voltage threshold and the resting membrane potential) was also unaffected in SOD1G93A vs. WT motoneurons (WT: 17.4 ± 7.3 mV; N = 48 vs. SOD1G93A: 18.2 ± 5.3 mV; N = 56; Mann-Whitney p=0.64; Figure 4C; and Table 2 for the distributions among motoneuron types).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claim: The gain (slope of frequency-current relationship in primary range) was unchanged in the whole population of motoneurons that fired during the ramp.
source: In the whole population of motoneurons that fired during the ramp, we found that the gain was unchanged (WT: 14 ± 6 Hz/nA; N = 43 vs. SOD1G93A: 17 ± 9 Hz/nA; N = 54 Mann-Whitney p=0.10; Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The motoneurons that become hypoexcitable by losing the ability to fire repetitively all belong to the FF motor units or the largest FR motor units.
source: Overall, our results show that the motoneurons that become hypoexcitable by losing the ability to fire repetitively all belong to the FF motor units or the largest FR motor units
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The remaining SOD1G93A motoneurons retain their normal excitability.
source: whereas the remaining SOD1G93A motoneurons retain their normal excitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the excitability measurements.

claim: Denervation of Tibialis Anterior (TA) in the τONFUSP525L mouse precedes denervation of TS.
source: In contrast to the SOD1G93A model, where denervation occurs fairly synchronously across hindlimb motor pools (Pun et al., 2006), denervation of Tibialis Anterior (TA, an ankle flexor muscle) in the 𝜏ONFUSP525L mouse precedes denervation of TS (an ankle extensor)(Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: The progression of denervation is much slower in τONFUSP525L than in SOD1G93A mice.
source: Moreover, the progression of the denervation is much slower in 𝜏ONFUSP525L than in SOD1G93A mice.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the cited literature.

claim: The TS motor unit properties in FUS mice were remarkably similar to those recorded in the SOD1G93A mouse, regardless of age.
source: Despite some small variations in twitch amplitudes, the TS motor unit properties were remarkably similar to those recorded in the SOD1G93A mouse, regardless of the age (compare Figure 2A–B and Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Motor units recorded from ankle flexors were all fast-contracting.
source: Consistent with the fact that TA and EDL are almost devoid of Type I muscle fibers (Wang and Kernell, 2001; Bloemberg and Quadrilatero, 2012), motor units recorded from the ankle flexors were all fast-contracting
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental observations.

claim: A large proportion of motoneurons in τONFUSP525L mice did not fire repetitively in response to a slow ramp of current.
source: As in SOD1G93A mice, we observed a large proportion of motoneurons in 𝜏ONFUSP525L mice that did not fire repetitively in response to a slow ramp of current (Figure 5A1)
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5A1.

claim: The loss of function in FUSP525L mice occurred at a time when the neuromuscular junctions are not denervated.
source: Again, this loss of function occurred at a time when the neuromuscular junctions are not denervated, as shown by the fact that an action potential elicited by a transient electrical pulse in the cell body elicits a motor unit action potential and a twitch of the motor unit (Figure 5A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A2.

claim: In ankle extensor motor pools, the proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically different between WT and mutant animals at P30 or P180.
source: In the ankle extensor motor pools, where denervation is the slowest, the proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically different between WT and mutant animals at either time point studied (Fisher exact test, p=0.69 at P30, p=1.00 at P180).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In ankle flexor motor pools at P30, the proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically significant between FUSP525L and FUSWT mice.
source: In the ankle flexor motor pools, the proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically significant at P30, when the denervation is just starting (Fisher exact test, p=0.43).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: At P180, there were significantly more non-repetitively-firing motoneurons in FUSP525L than in FUSWT mice (42% vs. 18%).
source: However, at P180, when the denervation is more advanced, there were significantly more non-repetitively-firing motoneurons in FUSP525L than in FUSWT mice (42% vs. 18%, respectively; Fisher exact test, p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In FF units of FUSP525L mice, 7/9 (78%) motoneurons were unable to fire repetitively.
source: In FF units, we found that 7/9 (78%) motoneurons were unable to fire repetitively (vs. 2/7, 17% in WT mice; Fisher exact test p=0.04).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: In FR units of FUSP525L mice, 7/22 (32%) motoneurons were unable to fire repetitively, which was not statistically different from WT mice.
source: In FR units (large and small taken together), we found that only 7/22 (32%) motoneurons were unable to fire repetitively, which was not statistically different from WT mice (4/21, 19%; Fisher exact test p=0.49).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: The proportion of non-firing motoneurons was much larger in large ankle flexor motor units in FUSP525L vs. FUSWT mice at P180 (13/19, 68% vs. 3/17, 18%).
source: when we split our samples between 'large' and 'small' motor units (based on the same cutoff value of 1.3 mN as used above, which is also the median twitch amplitude of FR ankle flexor units), the proportion of non-firing motoneuron was much larger in the large ankle flexor motor units in FUSP525L vs. FUSWT mice at P180 (13/19, 68% vs. 3/17, 18%, respectively; Fisher exact test, p=0.003)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: The proportion of non-firing motoneurons was not statistically different in small motor units between FUSP525L and FUSWT mice (WT: 2/10, 20% vs. FUS: 1/12, 8%).
source: whereas the proportion was not statistacally different in the small motor units (WT: 2/10, 20% vs. FUS: 1/12, 8%; Fisher exact test, p=0.57).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: The resting membrane potential of ankle flexor motoneurons at P180 tended to be more depolarized in non-firing cells than in cells able to fire repetitively, regardless of phenotype.
source: we observed that the resting membrane potential of ankle flexor motoneurons at P180 tended to be more depolarized in non-firing cells than in cells able to fire repetitively, regardless of the phenotype (FUSWT: non-firing −60 ± 7 mV; N = 6 vs. firing −72 ± 6 mV; N = 28; FUSP525L: non-firing −65 ± 7 mV; N = 15 vs. firing −70 ± 10 mV; N = 21; two-way ANOVA, p=0.001; Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The ankle flexor motoneurons that were able to fire repetitively at P180 retained normal excitability in FUSP525L mice.
source: Also in keeping with our results in the SOD1 model, the ankle flexor motoneurons that were able to fire repetitively at P180 retained normal excitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the excitability measurements.

claim: The recruitment current of firing motoneurons was not significantly different from controls in FUSP525L mice.
source: The recruitment current of the firing motoneurons was not significantly different from controls (FUSP525L: 7 ± 5 nA; N = 21 vs. FUSWT: 6 ± 4 nA; N = 28; Mann-Whitney p=0.87; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The slope of the relationship between recruitment current and input conductance was not affected by the FUS mutation.
source: Moreover, the slope of the relationship between recruitment current and input conductance was not affected by the mutation (ANCOVA p=0.19; Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Chodl was expressed in 8 out of 9 motoneurons innervating large motor units (twitch force larger than 1.3 mN).
source: In 19 WT TS motoneurons that we labeled intracellularly with neurobiotin during electrophysiological experiments (only one motoneuron was labeled per experiment)(Figure 7A), we found that Chodl was expressed in 8 out of 9 motoneurons innervating large motor units (twitch force larger than 1.3 mN, the median value of FR units, as used above)(Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments shown in Figures 7A, 7B, and 7D.

claim: Only 2 out of 10 motoneurons innervating smaller motor units expressed Chodl.
source: Only 2 out of 10 motoneurons innervating smaller motor units expressed Chodl.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: Chodl+ motor units developed 8.1 ± 8.6 mN of twitch force (range 1.0–29.8 mN; N = 10).
source: On average, Chodl+ motor units developed 8.1 ± 8.6 mN of twitch force (range 1.0–29.8 mN; N = 10)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: Chodl− motor units only developed 0.8 ± 0.6 mN of twitch force (range 0.4–2.2 mN; N = 9).
source: while Chodl− motor units only developed 0.8 ± 0.6 mN of twitch force (range 0.4–2.2 mN; N = 9; Mann-Whitney p<0.0001; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Chodl is expressed only in FF motoneurons and in FR motoneurons that innervate the largest motor units.
source: This shows that Chodl is expressed only in the FF motoneurons and in the FR motoneurons that innervate the largest motor units.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Chodl expression data.

claim: The FR motor units are not a homogeneous population, but can be separated into two subpopulations according to their size.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that the FR motor units are not a homogeneous population, but rather can be separated into two subpopulations according to their size.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Chodl expression and motor unit size data.

claim: p62 is an autophagy-substrate adapter involved in the degradation of mitochondria and aggregated misfolded proteins.
source: p62 is an autophagy-substrate adapter involved in the degradation of mitochondria and aggregated misfolded proteins (Matsumoto et al., 2015; Demishtein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: In the spinal cords of ALS mouse models, p62 accumulates over time.
source: In the spinal cords of ALS mouse models, p62 accumulates over time in ALS mouse models spinal cord (Zhang et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: p62-positive inclusions have been reported in vulnerable motoneurons.
source: and p62-positive inclusions have been reported in vulnerable motoneurons (Kaplan et al., 2014; Rudnick et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: p-eIF2α levels first increase in the most vulnerable motoneurons soon after the peak of ER stress markers is reached (about P37–42) and then decline back to baseline.
source: In the case of p-eIF2α, levels first increase in the most vulnerable motoneurons soon after the peak of ER stress markers is reached (about P37–42) and then decline back to baseline; p-eIF2α upregulation then follows in less vulnerable motoneurons (Saxena et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Eight motoneurons were recorded (four firing repetitively and four unable to do so) for disease marker analysis.
source: Altogether, we recorded eight motoneurons (four firing repetitively and four unable to do so).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: The recorded motoneurons were large cells and most likely belonged to large-sized motor units.
source: However, the recorded motoneurons were large cells and most likely belonged to large-sized motor units as they were large cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on cell size measurements.

claim: The soma cross-sectional area of the whole population of α-motoneurons in the imaged slices ranged from 80 to 1030 µm2 (420 ± 193 µm2; N = 279).
source: The soma cross-sectional area of the whole population of α-motoneurons in the imaged slices ranged from 80 to 1030 µm2 (420 ± 193 µm2; N = 279)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: All labeled motoneurons were larger than 490 µm2 (and up to 900 µm2; 704 ± 167 µm2; N = 8).
source: while all the labeled motoneurons were larger than 490 µm2 (and up to 900 µm2; 704 ± 167 µm2; N = 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: The non-repetitively-firing motoneurons had larger input conductances than the repetitively firing motoneurons (firing: 0.4 ± 0.1 µS; N = 4 vs. non-firing: 0.6 ± 0.1 µS; N = 4).
source: As previously, the non-repetitively-firing motoneurons had larger input conductances than the repetitively firing motoneurons (firing: 0.4 ± 0.1 µS; N = 4 vs. non-firing: 0.6 ± 0.1 µS; N = 4; Mann-Whitney p=0.030).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with statistical analysis.

claim: p-eIF2α was expressed in all NB-labeled motoneurons, while small, resistant size motoneurons were devoid of p-eIF2α.
source: As expected, p-eIF2α was expressed in all NB-labeled motoneurons, while small, resistant size motoneurons were devoid of p-eIF2α (Figure 8-Figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 8-Figure supplement 1.

claim: The levels of p-eIF2α were significantly higher in repetitively firing motoneurons than in motoneurons unable to fire repetitively.
source: However, the levels of p-eIF2α were significantly higher in repetitively firing motoneurons than in the motoneurons that were unable to fire repetitively (Figure 8A3 and B3; firing: 0.8 ± 0.2; N = 4 vs. non-firing: 0.2 ± 0.2; N = 4; Mann-Whitney p=0.02; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with statistical analysis shown in Figures 8A3, 8B3, and 8C.

claim: All NB-labeled motoneurons displayed p62 aggregates, in contrast to smaller neighboring motoneurons.
source: All the NB-labeled motoneurons displayed p62 aggregates, in contrast to smaller neighboring motoneurons, which did not (Figure 8-Figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 8-Figure supplement 1.

claim: In the four repetitively-firing NB-labeled motoneurons, p62 burden was moderate compared to some neighboring motoneurons.
source: However, in the four repetitively-firing NB-labeled motoneurons (from three different mice), p62 burden was moderate compared to some neighboring motoneurons that exhibited higher amounts of aggregates (figure 8A2).
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 8A2.

claim: Two non-repetitively-firing motoneurons displayed a p62 burden as high as in any of the neighboring motoneurons.
source: In the non-repetitively-firing motoneurons, p62 expression was more variable; two neurons, recorded in two different mice, displayed a p62 burden as high as in any of the neighboring motoneurons (Figure 8B2)
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 8B2.

claim: The non-firing, hypoexcitable state corresponds to a more advanced stage of the disease than the repetitive firing state.
source: Altogether, our results strongly suggest that the non-firing, hypoexcitable, state corresponds to a more advanced stage of the disease than the repetitive firing state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the p-eIF2α and p62 data.

claim: This is the first study in a mouse model of ALS to correlate changes in electrical properties of motoneurons with the physiological type of their motor unit.
source: For the first time in a mouse model of ALS, we have been able to correlate changes in the electrical properties of motoneurons with the physiological type of their motor unit.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study's approach.

claim: Motoneuron hypoexcitability is a loss of function that precedes the withdrawal of motor axons from the neuromuscular junction.
source: This study demonstrates that motoneuron hypoexcitability—as measured by the inability to fire repetitively—is a loss of function that precedes the withdrawal of motor axons from the neuromuscular junction, and is likely to be an early sign of motoneuron degeneration in ALS.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: Loss of repetitive discharge in response to a stationary stimulus develops progressively during ALS.
source: The loss of repetitive discharge in response to a stationary stimulus develops progressively during ALS.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the temporal progression observed in the data.

claim: From P30 to P60, 35% of motoneurons lose their ability to discharge repetitively.
source: From P30 to P60, 35% of the motoneurons lose their ability to discharge repetitively and the proportion was even larger at P80 (Delestrée et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The loss of ability to discharge repetitively is unrelated to anesthesia.
source: This loss of ability to discharge repetitively is unrelated to the anesthesia since it has also been found to occur in an in vitro preparation of adult sacrocaudal motoneurons in which no anesthetics were used, and in similar proportion as in lumbar motoneurons (Delestrée et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study that used different methods.

claim: A similar time-dependent transition between hyperexcitability to hypoexcitability has been documented in motoneurons derived from ALS patient iPSCs.
source: A similar time-dependent transition between hyperexcitability to hypoexcitability has been documented in motoneurons derived from ALS patient iPSCs.
evidence: This is a statement about findings in the literature.

claim: Four weeks after differentiation, patient-derived motor neurons with the SOD1A4V mutation are hyperexcitable.
source: Four weeks after differentiation, patient-derived motor neurons with the SOD1A4V mutation are hyperexcitable (more action potentials in response to a slow ramp depolarization) (Wainger et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claim: Loss of repetitive firing was observed 7–9 weeks after differentiation in patient-derived motor neurons with a SOD1 or a FUS mutation.
source: However, loss of repetitive firing was observed 7–9 weeks after differentiation in patient-derived motor neurons with a SOD1 or a FUS mutation (Naujock et al., 2016) or with a C9ORF72 repeat expansion (Sareen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claim: TARDBP or C9ORF72 cell lines transitioned over time from hyperexcitable to hypoexcitable.
source: Indeed, Devlin et al. (2015) showed that TARDBP or C9ORF72 cell lines transitioned over time from hyperexcitable (higher slope of the F-I function at two weeks post-plating) to hypoexcitable (inability to discharge a train starting from 7 to 8 weeks and proportion of hypoexcitable cells increasing later on).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claim: Loss of repetitive firing could be caused by an insufficient amount of sodium current, particularly its persistent component.
source: In mouse motoneurons, it has been suggested that loss of repetitive firing could be caused by an insufficient amount of sodium current, and most particularly of its persistent component (Delestrée et al., 2014), which is essential for the repetitive firing of spinal motoneurons (Harvey et al., 2006; Kuo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Motoneurons unable to fire repetitively were characterized by a large input conductance and a relatively small PIC.
source: They showed that, although the persistent inward current ('PIC', which includes the persistent sodium current) was generally strong in these motoneurons, the few motoneurons that were unable to fire repetitively were characterized by a large input conductance (i.e. large size, similarly to the present work) and a relatively small PIC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study by Huh et al. (2017).

claim: The late hypoexcitability in motoneurons derived from ALS patient iPSCs has been associated with an imbalance in sodium and potassium currents.
source: In motoneurons derived from ALS patient iPSCs, the late hypoexcitability has also been associated with an imbalance in the sodium and potassium currents, either a lower amount of sodium current or a larger amount of potassium current or both together (Sareen et al., 2014; Devlin et al., 2015; Naujock et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claim: A dysregulation of sodium alpha and beta subunits, or voltage-gated potassium channels, has been demonstrated in iPSC-derived motoneurons from ALS patients.
source: One cause for this imbalance might be a dysregulation of sodium alpha and beta subunits, or voltage-gated potassium channels, which have been demonstrated in iPSC-derived motoneurons from ALS patients (Sareen et al., 2014; Naujock et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: In motoneurons derived from TARDBP or C9ORF72 iPSC lines, the resting membrane potential was found to be more depolarized than in control lines.
source: In motoneurons derived from TARDBP or C9ORF72 iPSC lines, the resting membrane potential was found to be more depolarized than in control lines (Devlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claim: Reduced ATP availability in ALS can result in chronic membrane depolarization according to theoretical work.
source: The membrane depolarization reported in (Devlin et al., 2015); and this work) is consistent with the theoretical work by Le Masson et al. (2014) suggesting that reduced ATP availability in ALS can result in a chronic membrane depolarization.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a theoretical modeling study.

claim: In the Le Masson et al. model, membrane depolarization was largest at the axon distal extremity and returned closer to normal towards the soma.
source: In their model, Le Masson et al. (2014) found that the membrane depolarization was the largest at the axon distal extremity and that it returned closer to normal when going towards the soma.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a theoretical modeling study.

claim: Decreasing firing rate may prevent an energy crisis due to disruption of ATP production.
source: Le Masson et al. (2014) suggested that decreasing firing rate may prevent an energy crisis due to disruption of ATP production.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a theoretical modeling study.

claim: Retigabine, applied at an early stage when motoneurons derived from ALS patient iPSCs are hyperexcitable, increased their survival.
source: Retigabine, a specific opener of Kv7 channels—applied at an early stage, when motoneuron derived from ALS patient iPSCs are hyperexcitable—increased their survival (Wainger et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claim: Late treatment of hypoexcitable iPSC-derived motoneurons from ALS patients with 4-AP induces a decrease in ER stress and apoptosis markers.
source: In contrast, late treatment of hypoexcitable, iPSC-derived motoneurons from ALS patient with a potassium channel antagonist (4-AP) induces a decrease in ER stress and apoptosis markers (Naujock et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on iPSC-derived motoneurons.

claim: Early increase of motoneuron excitability in adult SOD1G93A mice decreases misfolded SOD burden, abolishes ER stress, and preserves muscle innervation.
source: In the same line, in vivo chemogenetic experiments in adult SOD1G93A mice suggested that an early increase of motoneuron—induced by expressing the cation-permeable PSAM (Magnus et al., 2011) before the onset of ER stress but after the appearance of misfolded SOD1—decreases misfolded SOD burden, abolishes ER stress and, upon protracted activation, negates the unfolded protein response and preserves muscle innervation (Saxena et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: Reducing motoneuron excitability has opposite effects to increasing excitability in SOD1G93A mice.
source: Conversely, reducing motoneuron excitability has opposite effects (Saxena et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study.

claim: Hypoexcitability contributes to motoneuron degeneration in ALS.
source: consistent with a model in which hypoexcitability contributes to motoneuron degeneration in ALS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited studies and the current work.

claim: The data support the role of hypoexcitability as a general mechanism contributing to motoneuron degeneration in ALS.
source: These data support the role of hypoexcitability as a general mechanism contributing to motoneuron degeneration in ALS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in two different ALS models.
